parsed_answer.content: Deciding where to persist a JSON Web Token (JWT) is a foundational architectural decision that pits convenience against hardened security. Local Storage is a client-side mechanism within the Web Storage API that is accessible via JavaScript. While it simplifies state management for Single Page Applications (SPAs), it is inherently vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks; if an attacker manages to inject a malicious script into your page, they can trivially exfiltrate your tokens via window.localStorage.getItem(). Conversely, HttpOnly cookies are a browser-level storage mechanism that prevents client-side scripts from accessing the cookie content. When the HttpOnly flag is set, the browser automatically attaches the cookie to outgoing requests, effectively shielding the token from XSS-based theft. However, using cookies introduces the risk of Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), as the browser will automatically include these cookies on requests to your domain, even if initiated by a third-party site. Mitigating this requires implementing SameSite=Strict or Lax attributes and robust CSRF protection tokens, which are standard in frameworks like Spring Security.

items: Local Storage persists until explicitly cleared, making it a persistent target for attackers who gain execution context in your SPA.
HttpOnly cookies leverage the browser's native cookie jar, ensuring that even if an XSS payload executes, the document.cookie object remains empty of your sensitive JWT.
Spring Security's CSRF protection is mandatory when using cookies, typically requiring a hidden token that the client must echo back in a custom header to validate the request origin.
SameSite=Strict cookie attribute prevents the browser from sending the cookie on cross-site requests, which is the primary defense against CSRF in modern browsers.

parsed_answer.content: The 'Gold Standard' for production is often a hybrid approach: Store the JWT in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie to prevent XSS, and use a secondary CSRF token (often stored in memory or a non-HttpOnly cookie) to validate that the request originated from your own frontend. Never rely on Local Storage for sensitive authentication tokens in a production environment if you care about PCI-DSS or SOC2 compliance.

title: Where should you store a JWT on the client side? (Local Storage vs HttpOnly Cookies)
